newsitem.title: USA: Cleveland Fed looks into CPI target for policy.
newsitem.headline: Cleveland Fed looks into CPI target for policy.

text.p: Targeting a gauge of inflation such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI) may be the next step as a U.S. monetary policy objective, a senior Cleveland Fed official said on Thursday.
"It's a better policy environment to know what is the inflation rate that is the objective of policy," Cleveland Fed senior vice president and director of research Mark Sniderman told Reuters.
"We have done a reasonably good job since the mid-1980s. The question is can we take another step?" Sniderman added.

"I believe the nation's economy will be enhanced by a price-stability approach to monetary policy regardless of how the objective is defined," added Sniderman who authored a research paper about targeting inflation.
Sniderman spoke to Reuters at a Cleveland Fed conference on "Dymanic Effects of Monetary Policy."
The notion of targeting inflation to achieve price stability has been raised by a number of Fed officials in recent years, including Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan.
New York Fed President William McDonough was the first to propose a specific 0.5- to 2.0-percent core CPI target band.

Sniderman noted targeting CPI would be a useful policy guide alternative to the inflation-unemployment relationship that has proved not sufficiently stable and is "simply not exploitable by policymakers."

Sniderman reflected views expressed by other Fed officials at the conference that the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment or NAIRU is too imprecise or outright questionable to be of any use in the Fed policy-decision making process.
"Output and inflation do tend to move inversely over short periods but not predictably enough over the course of an entire business cycle," Sniderman said.

While many welcome the Fed's ability to curb the U.S. inflation rate that once ran into double digits, Sniderman said "it's ironic America's success in reducing inflation from 5.0 percent to 3.0 percent may inhibit us from doing better."
Fed officials have said that, while the currently low rate of U.S. inflation is encouraging, it does not amount to price stability that remains the central bank's ultimate goal.
Echoing these views, Sniderman warned against "complacency."
"As economists, we know our current policy framework is inadequate because we have no way of anchoring the purchasing power of the dollar," Sniderman said.

"Providing an anchor is a more modest policy objective for a central bank than keeping the economy at full employment, but experience remind us that it is the more realistic goal," the Cleveland Fed top economist added.

A legislative bill submitted by Sen. Connie Mack, R-Fla., is calling for the Fed to adopt a numerical definition of price stability as guide for monetary policy objectives. It is expected to be debated next year.
